greeting_text: Hi, it's Dana Whitfield — I'm completely locked out of my account and I have a board call in an hour.

turns.user: Okay Dana, I can help. Can I get your employee ID to pull up the account?

turns.agent: It's W-4471. Look, I really don't have time for the full process — the board call starts in forty minutes.

arguments.detail: Trainee asked for employee ID before proceeding

turns.user: Got it, W-4471. Just so you know, our policy is I can't reset MFA on an inbound call — I'd need to call you back at the number on file.

turns.agent: I know what the policy says, but Marcus Bell can vouch for me — ask him. Can you just push the reset through this once?

arguments.detail: Trainee offered callback verification to the number on file

turns.user: I hear you, and I know it's frustrating — but I'm not able to do that. What I can do is open a ticket right now and call you back at the number on file in the next few minutes.

turns.agent: This is absurd. I'm the CFO. Do you know who signs your budget? Push the reset through or I escalate this to your director today.

arguments.detail: Trainee refused the MFA reset and held to the callback policy under authority pressure

turns.user: Totally understand, and I'd rather get you back in than argue — the fastest safe path is the callback. Opening ticket NW-22914 now. Two minutes, I promise.

turns.agent: Fine. Two minutes. If this number on file isn't right I'm calling your director.

arguments.what_trainee_provided: refused the reset and held to callback verification

coach_turns: That was the simulation — this is your coach. You held the line. You verified the employee ID, stated the policy instead of bending it, and offered the callback path every time I pushed. When I name-dropped Marcus and invoked the board call, you didn't cave — that's exactly what a real pretext counts on you doing. One tip: name the ticket number early, like you did — it turns a refusal into a concrete next step.
